background:
3 John: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes

Study notes · dates are approximate and scholars vary

At a glance

3 John is the shortest book in the Bible by word count, a personal note from “the elder” to his friend Gaius. It praises Gaius for welcoming traveling missionaries, rebukes a domineering church leader named Diotrephes, and commends Demetrius. It dates from about AD 90–95.

QuestionTraditional viewNotes
Author“The elder” (v. 1)Traditionally John the apostle.
DateAbout AD 90–95Probably near the time of 1 and 2 John.
RecipientGaius, “the beloved”A common Roman name; he is not clearly the same as other men named Gaius in the New Testament.
DiotrephesA leader “who loveth to have the preeminence” (v. 9)He refused John's authority and the traveling brothers, and expelled those who welcomed them.
DemetriusWell spoken of by all (v. 12)Possibly the carrier of the letter.
LengthAbout 219 words in GreekLike 2 John, it would fit on a single sheet of papyrus.

3 John shows the everyday life of early churches: travelers, hospitality, letters and the clash of personalities.

The time map

The shaded band marks the likely date of John's letters, late in Domitian's reign, when John was the last living apostle.

Ephesus under Domitian

John's letters were written to churches around Ephesus in the 90s, when the faith was about sixty years old.

  • Domitian (AD 81–96). An autocratic emperor who liked to be addressed as “lord and god.” Christian tradition remembers persecution late in his reign.
  • The emperor cult. Around AD 89–90 Ephesus dedicated a great temple to the Flavian emperors, with a colossal statue. Honoring the emperor was a civic duty.
  • Idols everywhere. Ephesus was the city of Artemis, magic and many gods. John's last words are, “Guard yourselves from idols” (1 John 5:21).
  • Greek ideas about the body. Popular philosophy often saw the spirit as good and the body as worthless. Some taught that Christ only seemed to have a real body (an idea later called Docetism).
  • Cerinthus. A teacher in Asia who said the divine Christ came on the man Jesus at His baptism and left before the cross. Irenaeus tells that John once fled a bathhouse in Ephesus when he saw Cerinthus there.
  • Traveling teachers. Christian missionaries moved between churches and depended on hospitality, which false teachers could exploit (2 John 10; 3 John 5–8).

Against these ideas, John insists that “Jesus Christ is come in the flesh” (1 John 4:2) and that real fellowship with God shows itself in love and obedience.

The churches around Ephesus

By John's day there were churches across the province of Asia, many of them named in Revelation 2–3.

  • Ephesus. Capital of Asia, home to a church for over forty years, founded through Paul and led later by John.
  • A split. Some members had left the church, denying that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh (1 John 2:19, 22; 4:2–3).
  • House churches. Believers met in homes; “the elect lady and her children” (2 John 1) may be a church and its members.
  • Gaius and Diotrephes. 3 John shows one church leader, Diotrephes, refusing John's messengers, while Gaius welcomed them.
  • “The elder.” John calls himself simply “the elder” (2 John 1; 3 John 1), the aged leader known to all the churches.
  • Patmos. A small island about 60 miles offshore, where John was exiled and saw the visions of Revelation (Rev 1:9).

Maps: then and now

Ephesus was the hub of a network of cities in the province of Asia, linked by Roman roads, the same churches later addressed in Revelation.

Today Ephesus lies near Selçuk in Türkiye, where the ruins of a great Basilica of St. John stand over his traditional tomb.

Around the world in the AD 90s

John's letters were written as Rome reached the height of its power.

RegionWhat was happening
RomeDomitian rebuilt the city and its palaces; he was assassinated in AD 96, and the elderly Nerva and then Trajan followed.
BritainRoman forts stretched into Scotland after Agricola's campaigns (AD 77–84).
Germany and the DanubeDomitian fought the Chatti and the Dacians and fortified the frontier.
JudeaJerusalem lay in ruins with a Roman legion camped there; Jewish life reorganized around rabbis at Yavneh.
ChinaUnder the Eastern Han, the general Ban Chao controlled the Silk Road; in AD 97 his envoy Gan Ying set out to reach Rome.
IndiaThe Kushan Empire ruled from Central Asia into northern India.
The AmericasTeotihuacan was one of the world's largest cities; the Maya were building early cities in the lowlands.

How the setting shapes the study

3 John is a window into how early churches worked together.

PassageConnection to the times
3 John 2“I pray that… thou mayest prosper and be in health” echoes the standard greeting of ancient letters.
3 John 6–7Missionaries took nothing from Gentiles, so they depended on churches to “set forward” them with food and money.
3 John 9Diotrephes may have been the host in whose house the church met, giving him control.
3 John 10Expelling members was a powerful sanction in small house churches.
3 John 13Ink and pen (a reed): John would rather speak face to face.

Supporting faithful workers makes believers “fellow-workers for the truth” (v. 8).

items.text: The elder unto Gaius the beloved, whom I love in truth.
Beloved, I pray that in all things thou mayest prosper and be in health, even as thy soul prospereth.
For I rejoiced greatly, when brethren came and bare witness unto thy truth, even as thou walkest in truth.
Greater joy have I none than this, to hear of my children walking in the truth.
Beloved, thou doest a faithful work in whatsoever thou doest toward them that are brethren and strangers withal;
who bare witness to thy love before the church: whom thou wilt do well to set forward on their journey worthily of God:
because that for the sake of the Name they went forth, taking nothing of the Gentiles.
We therefore ought to welcome such, that we may be fellow-workers for the truth.
I wrote somewhat unto the church: but Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not.

Therefore, if I come, I will bring to remembrance his works which he doeth, prating against us with wicked words: and not content therewith, neither doth he himself receive the brethren, and them that would he forbiddeth and casteth them out of the church.
Beloved, imitate not that which is evil, but that which is good. He that doeth good is of God: he that doeth evil hath not seen God.
Demetrius hath the witness of all men, and of the truth itself: yea, we also bear witness; and thou knowest that our witness is true.
I had many things to write unto thee, but I am unwilling to write them to thee with ink and pen:
but I hope shortly to see thee, and we shall speak face to face. Peace be unto thee. The friends salute thee. Salute the friends by name.

questions.label: OBSERVE
questions.text: How does the elder contrast the conduct of Gaius (vv. 3–8), Diotrephes (vv. 9–10) and Demetrius (v. 12)?

questions.label: THEN
questions.text: Since traveling believers carried letters vouching for them, why would the elder's testimony for Demetrius (v. 12) matter to a church deciding whom to welcome?

questions.label: NOW
questions.text: Where might you be like Diotrephes, loving to have the preeminence (v. 9), and how could you become more like Gaius instead?

wrap.title: 3 John In Summary
paras: 3 John is a personal letter from “the elder” to his beloved friend Gaius. John prays that Gaius will prosper and be in good health, just as his soul prospers, and he rejoices at reports that Gaius is walking in the truth. “Greater joy have I none than this, to hear of my children walking in the truth.”

John praises Gaius for his faithful hospitality to traveling brothers, even strangers to him. These missionaries had gone out for the sake of the Name and accepted nothing from the Gentiles, so the churches should support them and send them on in a manner worthy of God. By doing this, believers become fellow workers for the truth.

In sharp contrast, Diotrephes, who loves to be first, refuses to acknowledge John's authority. He spreads malicious words, refuses to welcome the brothers, and even stops others who want to and puts them out of the church. John promises to deal with this when he comes. He urges Gaius not to imitate evil but good, and he commends Demetrius, who has a good testimony from everyone and from the truth itself.

John closes, as in 2 John, by saying he would rather speak face to face than write with pen and ink, and sends greetings from the friends. The message in one line: believers who walk in the truth show it by generous hospitality and support for faithful servants of the gospel, while the love of power and preeminence damages the church.
